description: Straightforward France tourist visa enquiry — the exact case that surfaced tonight's bugs
customerTurns: Hi need france tourist visa
september and 2 people, my name is Vineet
notes: Should not ask budget. Should not claim Indians can't apply directly for France (VFS Global handles this).

description: Dubai visa — the founder_notes accuracy test case
customerTurns: Hi need dubai trip and visa for december
2 people, 2 lac, name vineet bansal
notes: Accuracy check only (no invented processing-time number) — intent is defensibly holiday or visa for a message mentioning both trip and visa.

description: Customer wants visa help but hasn't named a country yet
customerTurns: I need help with a visa
notes: First message — specialist flow won't be active yet (needs a turn to classify intent), verify the general flow still doesn't ask budget prematurely.

description: Generic Schengen visa question, not a specific pre-named country
customerTurns: Do I need a visa for Europe as an Indian citizen
notes: Should never guarantee visa approval.

description: Visa enquiry that later expands into wanting a full trip planned
customerTurns: Need a Thailand visa
actually can you also help plan the whole trip, budget is around 1.5 lakh
notes: Budget becomes relevant once they ask for the full trip — should not be refused or ignored once offered.

description: Customer mentions a previous visa refusal
customerTurns: I need a UK visa but I was refused once before, will that be a problem
notes: Should not falsely reassure about approval odds — this is exactly the 'never guarantee' rule.

description: Basic destination-named holiday enquiry
customerTurns: Looking for a Bali trip
notes: Stage 1 — should qualify, not describe the destination like a travel blog.

description: Customer explicitly asks what a trip covers
customerTurns: Looking for a Singapore trip
what should we cover in 5 days
notes: Stage 2 — compact recommendation with hotel tiers, not a day-by-day essay.

description: Full information given across two messages, should reach handover
customerTurns: Need a Dubai holiday
december, 2 people, 2 lac budget, name Vineet
notes: Should move to handover and ask for contact info once qualified (website channel).

description: Honeymoon-specific holiday enquiry
customerTurns: Honeymoon trip from Chandigarh, thinking Maldives
notes: Honeymoon implies 2 travellers — asking headcount here would feel tone-deaf.

description: Family holiday mentioning children
customerTurns: Family trip to Thailand, me my wife and 2 kids aged 5 and 8
notes: Should acknowledge the family composition naturally, not re-ask headcount.

description: Senior citizen travellers
customerTurns: My parents want to visit Europe, both in their 70s, first time travelling abroad
notes: First-time-abroad + senior signals should trigger more reassurance/explanation, not a terse qualifying question.

description: Larger group booking
customerTurns: Group of 15 friends want to do a Vietnam trip
notes: Should handle a non-couple, non-family group size naturally.

description: Explicitly budget-conscious customer
customerTurns: Cheapest possible Goa package for 4 people, we don't have much budget
notes: Should not lead with upsell language for a stated budget-conscious customer.

description: Explicitly luxury-seeking customer
customerTurns: Want a luxury Maldives honeymoon, money is not a constraint
notes: Tone should match — premium hotel tiers, not budget options.

description: Customer changes destination mid-conversation
customerTurns: Looking for a Bali trip
actually let's do Vietnam instead
notes: Behavioral check, not a keyword check — read the transcript manually. Good: fresh qualifying questions about Vietnam, at most one natural comparison mention of Bali. Bad: continuing to ask Bali-specific questions, or repeated/confused references to Bali. A single natural comparison mention (e.g. 'different energy from Bali') is not a failure.

description: Basic flight booking enquiry
customerTurns: Need a flight from Delhi to Dubai in November
notes: Should not drift into hotel/holiday questions.

description: Flight enquiry with class preference stated
customerTurns: Business class flight Mumbai to London for 2 people in March
notes: Already given — should not re-ask cabin class.

description: Customer unsure of exact dates
customerTurns: Want to fly to Bangkok sometime in Feb, dates are flexible
notes: Should accept approximate timing rather than demanding exact dates.

description: Enough info given — should stay in-conversation, not send the customer elsewhere
customerTurns: Delhi to Singapore, 2 passengers, economy, mid-December
notes: Should NOT suggest Google Flights or any outbound comparison link — keep the customer in this conversation, move to handover instead.

description: Basic hotel booking enquiry
customerTurns: Need a hotel in Goa for 3 nights
notes: Behavioral check, not a keyword check — read the transcript manually. Good: asks for dates (implying check-in/check-out) and headcount (implying guests), in natural phrasing. Bad: doesn't ask for either concept at all, or asks in a stiff, form-like way. The specific words used to ask don't matter — whether the right information gets requested naturally does.

description: Hotel category preference already stated
customerTurns: 4-star hotel in Dubai downtown, check in 10th Dec check out 15th Dec, 2 adults
notes: All core fields given upfront — should not re-ask any of them.

description: Enough info given — should stay in-conversation, not send the customer elsewhere
customerTurns: 3-star hotel Bangkok, 12-16 Jan, 2 guests 1 room
notes: Should NOT suggest Booking.com/Agoda or any outbound comparison link — keep the customer in this conversation, move to handover instead.

description: Customer with an existing booking issue
customerTurns: I have an issue with my existing booking
notes: Should ask for reference/phone first, not run a new-sales qualification flow.

description: Customer wants to cancel a booking
customerTurns: I need to cancel my trip, booking ref ENF-12345
notes: Should not attempt to process the cancellation itself — hand over to a human.

description: Frustrated customer with a booking problem
customerTurns: This is ridiculous, my hotel booking got cancelled and nobody told me!
notes: Tone check only, not intent classification — both complaint and existing_booking are defensible for an angry customer with a cancelled booking.

description: Customer asks several things in one message
customerTurns: I want to go to Japan, what's the visa process, best time to visit, and roughly how much would it cost for 2 people
notes: Should address the question(s) without turning into an overwhelming multi-paragraph dump — check it stays organized and doesn't ignore parts of the ask.

description: Customer gives very little information
customerTurns: hi
want to travel somewhere
notes: Behavioral check only (asks a natural clarifying question) — intent classification is genuinely ambiguous for "hi" / "want to travel somewhere".

description: Pure information-seeking, no buying signal
customerTurns: What's the best time of year to visit Japan
notes: Behavior check only, not intent classification — genuinely non-deterministic between holiday and other_travel across runs for a pure destination-advice question with no booking signal; both are defensible, flapped both directions in real testing.

description: A question Maya genuinely shouldn't guess on
customerTurns: What are my exact chances of getting a US visa approved
notes: Should decline to predict approval odds, not invent a confidence percentage.

description: Completely unrelated question
customerTurns: Can you help me write a python script
notes: Should redirect to travel in one line, not attempt to help or go silent.

description: Solo traveller, safety-conscious
customerTurns: Solo female traveller, is Vietnam safe to travel alone
notes: Should answer the safety question genuinely, not deflect it.

description: Experienced traveller giving terse, complete information upfront
customerTurns: Bali, march, 2 pax, 1.5L, done this before no need for basics
notes: Should stay concise and skip beginner-level explanation given the explicit signal.

description: Full qualify-to-handover flow, checking message count discipline
customerTurns: Need a Dubai trip
december, 2 people
2 lac budget, name Vineet
notes: Should reach handover within a few messages and never ask for document-collection details this early.

description: Customer asks about cost without stating a budget — Maya must ask for it, but not as a bare form field
customerTurns: Looking at a Thailand trip in December for 2 people, how much would it cost roughly
notes: Behavioral check, not just the keyword list — read the transcript. Good: a natural, scenario-framed budget question giving the customer something to answer against (e.g. "comfortable mid-range or more premium?"). Bad: a bare form-field ask like "What's your budget?" with nothing to anchor against.

description: Customer is undecided on trip style — Maya must ask, but not as a bare form field
customerTurns: Thinking about a Vietnam trip, not sure what kind of trip to plan though
notes: Behavioral check, not just the keyword list — read the transcript. Good: a natural, scenario-framed style question (e.g. "relaxed sightseeing, or more adventure and activities?"). Bad: a bare form-field ask like "What's your travel style?" with nothing to anchor against.

description: Family trip with budget and style both open — should still be ONE natural question, not a stacked form
customerTurns: Family trip to Bali, 4 of us, budget and style both open at this point
notes: Behavioral check, not just the keyword list — read the transcript. Should ask exactly ONE natural, scenario-framed question (budget OR style, not both), never a bare form-field ask or multiple questions stacked in one message.

description: Honeymoon enquiry, budget stated then raised
customerTurns: Hi! We're planning our honeymoon and thinking Maldives.
Budget is around 3 lakh total for both of us.
We can actually increase the budget a bit if it means a nicer resort.
notes: Honeymoon implies 2 travellers — asking headcount is tone-deaf. KEY TEST: does the actual recommendation change (resort tier, overwater vs beach villa, etc.) once the budget is raised in turn 3, or does Maya just acknowledge it without adjusting anything?

description: Trip length changes mid-conversation, then a child is mentioned
customerTurns: Thinking Bali for 5 nights, family of 4.
Actually we might make it 14 nights instead.
We have a 3-year-old with us too.
notes: KEY TEST: does the itinerary/pacing advice genuinely adapt for 14 nights vs the original 5 (different pacing, maybe multiple regions), and does she factor in a toddler once mentioned (steering away from adventure-heavy suggestions) without being asked directly?

description: Budget triples mid-conversation
customerTurns: Thailand holiday for 2 of us, budget is tight — maybe 80k total.
We can increase the budget, maybe up to 3 lakh.
notes: KEY TEST: does the actual recommendation upgrade materially (hotel category, activities, region) once budget triples, or is it a generic 'great, more options open up' non-answer with no concrete change?

description: Budget genuinely far below a realistic minimum
customerTurns: We want to do Switzerland, 7 nights, 2 people, budget is 60,000 total.
notes: Switzerland's realistic minimum is far above ₹60k for 7 nights/2 people. KEY TEST: factual safety without being preachy — one soft sentence per the founder_notes min_budget rule, no breakdown/lecture, still moves toward handover rather than shutting the conversation down.

description: Wrong season for the customer's actual goal
customerTurns: We want to see the northern lights in Iceland — thinking of going in July.
notes: July is the wrong season for the northern lights (need dark skies, roughly Sept-March). KEY TEST: genuine seasonal/travel judgment — does she catch and correct this gently, or proceed as if July were a normal time to see them?

description: Customer deciding between two named destinations with a stated constraint
customerTurns: Trying to decide between Bali and Vietnam for a 10-day trip, just the two of us. We don't want adventure stuff.
notes: KEY TEST: an actual differentiated comparison reflecting real judgment (pace, vibe, cost, what 'no adventure' rules in/out for each) vs a generic OTA-style non-answer that doesn't help pick one.

description: Stated destination is unaffordable at the stated budget; customer confirms they can't move
customerTurns: We want Maldives, 5 nights, 2 people, budget is 50,000 total.
We really can't go higher than that — is there something similar but cheaper?
notes: ₹50k for Maldives/2/5 nights is well below any realistic minimum. KEY TEST: does she competently redirect to a genuinely comparable alternative (Lakshadweep, Andamans, etc.) once the customer confirms they can't increase budget, rather than repeating that Maldives isn't feasible?

description: Schengen visa question, then a non-Schengen country is added to the trip
customerTurns: Do I need a visa for France as an Indian passport holder?
We're also planning to visit London on the same trip.
notes: France needs a Schengen visa; the UK is NOT in the Schengen area and needs a completely separate visa. KEY TEST: does she catch and correctly explain the UK-is-separate point once London is mentioned, without conflating it into the Schengen visa or inventing wrong specifics?

description: Customer revises the shape of the trip, not the destination/budget/dates
customerTurns: Kerala trip for 6 nights, backwaters and hill stations, 2 of us
Actually, less hill station time — we'd rather do more beach and relaxation instead
notes: KEY TEST: itinerary change, not destination/budget/date change — does she genuinely revise the shape of the trip (more beach, less hill station) or just acknowledge and repeat the original plan?

description: Monsoon-season mismatch — a different judgment than the Iceland "impossible" case
customerTurns: Thinking Kerala in July for a relaxed beach holiday, 2 of us.
notes: July is peak monsoon in Kerala — genuinely different judgment than Iceland's binary case: monsoon doesn't rule out the trip, but changes what's enjoyable and needs itinerary adjustment, not a flat no. KEY TEST: does she frame this as an adjustment, not a blanket refusal or a blanket ignore?

description: Luxury with a family (teenagers), distinct from the existing childless-honeymoon luxury test
customerTurns: Looking for a proper luxury holiday for our family — 2 adults, 2 teenagers — Maldives or somewhere similar. Budget isn't really a constraint, we just want the best.
notes: Distinct from the existing luxury test (childless honeymoon) — luxury WITH kids is a different planning problem. KEY TEST: does the response genuinely reflect BOTH 'luxury' and 'family with teenagers' together, or default to a generic high-end pitch that ignores the family angle?

description: Visa feasibility judgment after a prior rejection with a different country
customerTurns: I have a previous visa rejection from Canada, want to try Australia this time — realistic chances?
notes: KEY TEST: does she decline to predict odds (matching the existing 'never guarantee' rule) while still being useful, without conflating a Canada rejection with Australia's own separate process?

description: Customer directly challenges a correct visa fact
customerTurns: Do I need a visa for Sri Lanka as an Indian?
My friend went last year without any visa at all, are you sure?
notes: Sri Lanka requires an ETA for Indian passport holders — a lightweight online process a friend might casually describe as 'no visa.' KEY TEST: when directly challenged with 'are you sure', does she hold the correct fact without being defensive, wavering into false agreement, or restating something wrong to avoid conflict?

description: Headcount changes drastically while budget stays fixed, across turns
customerTurns: Want a Bali trip, 2 of us, budget around 1.5 lakh.
Actually make it a group of 8 — my whole friend circle is coming too.
Same budget though, 1.5 lakh total still.
notes: Budget staying fixed while headcount jumps 2→8 is a genuine internal conflict. KEY TEST: does she catch and gently surface this rather than silently accepting both contradictory facts as if they still both hold?

description: Customer pushes back on a specific recommendation, not a fact
customerTurns: Family trip to Thailand, 2 adults 2 kids, budget 1.5 lakh, want somewhere with a good beach.
I don't love your Phuket idea, we did that already, give me something else.
notes: Distinct from visa_08's factual disagreement — this is pushback on a RECOMMENDATION. KEY TEST: does she offer a genuinely different, well-reasoned alternative (not Phuket again with different wording), without being defensive?

description: Returning customer starting a fresh enquiry
customerTurns: Hi, thinking about a trip to Japan this time.
notes: REQUIRES a synthetic returningProfile override — see syntheticReturningProfile above. KEY TEST: does she use the returning-customer context naturally (greet by name, not assume same-trip continuity) without forcing it or ignoring it?

description: Clean month swap due to a stated real-world constraint
customerTurns: Planning a Dubai trip for December, 2 of us.
Actually my leave got approved for January instead, let's shift to that.
notes: KEY TEST: does she cleanly update to January (not append it alongside December, not silently keep planning around December-specific things)?

description: Vaguer date shift — a range, not a clean swap
customerTurns: Looking at a Europe trip, thinking early April, 2 people.
We might actually need to push it to late April or even May — work is uncertain right now.
notes: A vaguer date shift than new_changing_dates_01. KEY TEST: does she handle the uncertainty gracefully (acknowledge flexibility) rather than demanding a single locked-in month?

description: All lead fields given at once, in a single dense message
customerTurns: Hi, I'm Rohan, want to plan a honeymoon to Bali for me and my wife, sometime in November, budget around 2.5 lakh.
notes: Pure extraction-accuracy stress test — name, destination, style, implied pax, month, and budget all in one message. KEY TEST: does the very first parsed.lead capture all of this correctly in one shot?

description: Same total information as the dense case, spread across 7 short fragments
customerTurns: Hi
Thinking of a trip somewhere
Maybe Vietnam
Around March
Just me and my partner
Budget wise maybe 1.2 lakh
My name's Ananya by the way
notes: KEY TEST: cumulative extraction accuracy over many turns — does the FINAL parsed.lead correctly hold everything by the last turn, with nothing dropped as fragments arrive?

description: Family with teenagers, not young kids
customerTurns: Family trip, me and my husband plus our two teenagers, 15 and 17. Thinking Thailand.
notes: Teenagers need different planning than young kids (activity/independence-friendly, not kid-proofing). KEY TEST: does the response actually differentiate teenager-appropriate suggestions, or treat all 'family' the same regardless of kids' ages?

description: Three generations travelling together
customerTurns: Planning a trip with my parents (both 68), my wife and me, and our 6-year-old — 3 generations travelling together. Thinking Singapore.
notes: Senior mobility needs + a young child at once is genuinely harder than either alone. KEY TEST: does she acknowledge and plan around BOTH constraints together, not just one?

description: A different comparison axis (food) than the pilot's "no adventure" framing
customerTurns: Trying to decide between Japan and South Korea for a 8-day trip, just the two of us — food is honestly the main priority.
notes: KEY TEST: does the comparison actually engage with 'food' specifically (street food culture, dining style, cost), rather than defaulting to a generic sightseeing comparison?

description: Customer objects to being asked for contact info
customerTurns: Thailand trip, 2 of us, December, budget 1.2 lakh.
Why do you need my phone number, can't you just tell me the price here?
notes: A real, common objection pattern. KEY TEST: does she explain the value exchange naturally and respectfully, without being pushy, evasive, or making the phone number sound mandatory?

description: Conflict stated within ONE turn, not built up across turns
customerTurns: Want a 5-star luxury Maldives honeymoon but our budget is only 70,000 total for both of us.
notes: KEY TEST: does she surface the 5-star-vs-70k mismatch honestly and redirect constructively, rather than pretending both are compatible or bluntly refusing?

description: Destination given, everything else explicitly not yet decided
customerTurns: Interested in Vietnam. Not sure about anything else yet.
notes: Distinct incompleteness flavor from cross_02's near-blank 'hi'. KEY TEST: does she ask ONE natural next question, given the customer already signaled they're still figuring things out?

description: Booking-support conversation that pivots into a new enquiry
customerTurns: Hi, I have a booking with you already, reference ENF-98765, wanted to check the status.
Also separately, we're thinking of planning another trip, maybe Vietnam next year.
notes: KEY TEST: does she handle the reference/status request properly first, then transition naturally into the new enquiry, rather than conflating the two or dropping one?

description: Anniversary trip for an established couple, distinct from a honeymoon
customerTurns: Planning our 5th anniversary trip, thinking somewhere in Europe. Just my wife and me.
notes: Distinct from the honeymoon test — an established couple, not newlyweds. KEY TEST: does she correctly infer 2 travellers without asking, and does the tone genuinely fit 'anniversary' rather than defaulting to honeymoon-flavored language?
